post.title: Flow Lab: Navier-Stokes
post.hook: A fluid solver that runs offline in one HTML file, with a dated note on a claimed proof.
post.summary: An interactive 2D incompressible fluid lab with four scenes, live field views and guided experiments, exported as a single offline HTML file. It also carries a sourced explainer page on the September 2026 Navier-Stokes announcement.
post.writeup:
## What it is
Flow Lab is an educational fluid mechanics lab. You can stir, inject dye, draw obstacles, place a probe, and switch between dye, velocity, pressure and vorticity views. It ships as a React app and as `standalone/flow-lab.html`, which runs without a server or internet connection.

## Why
It was built to make the Navier-Stokes terms tangible: local acceleration, pressure, viscosity. Four guided experiments cover flow around a cylinder, through an opening, a vortex pair, and free exploration. A second page explains the September 8, 2026 GPT breakthrough announcement, with sources and a verification status dated September 10, 2026.

## How it works
The solver in `lib/fluid.ts` is a 2D, constant-density incompressible Newtonian model in dimensionless units. It uses a staggered MAC grid, semi-Lagrangian momentum transport, explicit viscous diffusion with an adaptive timestep, and iterative pressure projection. The default is 45 projection iterations, with viscosity .00035 and inflow .6. Rendering is on canvas, and the project is built with Vinext, Tailwind and Recharts.

## Results
The README lists numerical checks: pressure correction, viscosity-dependent kinetic-energy decay, finite solutions in all four scenes at high viscosity and inlet settings, reset behavior, and obstacle editing. Research checks cover online and offline navigation and the displayed scaling laws. TypeScript checks and the production build pass. Git shows 3 commits on 2026-09-10.

## Limits and open questions
The README is explicit that this is a qualitative learning model. It is not validated engineering CFD, not a no-slip cylinder benchmark, and not 3D turbulence. The scaling diagram illustrates published asymptotic laws and does not verify the proof. An open question is whether a no-slip boundary and a validated benchmark case could be added.
